opening.text: Picture a rocky coast on a dark night. The sea is rough. A small boat is far from shore, and the captain cannot see land. Then, on the horizon, a light appears. It turns slowly. It is not close, and it does not make the waves smaller. But it tells the captain two things. Land is there. And there is a safe way in.
That is what hope is like. It is a light that shows us where we are going when we cannot yet see the shore.
Today I want to talk about hope. What it is, where it comes from, and how it helps us in the dark.

mainMessage.text: Hope is not wishing. It is not a hunch that things might turn out fine. Hope in the gospel is a steady trust that the Lord will keep His promises. It rests on Jesus Christ, and it grows out of faith.
Hope matters because life is not always easy. People lose jobs. Families face illness and loss. We make mistakes and feel far from God. In those moments, hope is what keeps us from giving up.
We will look at six parts. What hope is. Where it holds us. How it helps in trials. How it helps after sin. How it fills us with joy. And what it looks forward to.

blocks.text: Let us start with a simple question. What is hope?
Paul gave a short description that connects it to faith.
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
Faith and hope belong together. Hope looks ahead to what is promised. Faith gives it substance. We cannot see the shore yet, but we trust that it is there.
Mormon taught this in a letter written by his son Moroni. He asked a question that is worth sitting with.

And again, my beloved brethren, I would speak unto you concerning hope. How is it that ye can attain unto faith, save ye shall have hope?
And what is it that ye shall hope for? Behold I say unto you that ye shall have hope through the atonement of Christ and the power of his resurrection, to be raised unto life eternal, and this because of your faith in him according to the promise.

How can we have faith without hope? We cannot. And what do we hope for? The answer is plain. We hope through the Atonement of Christ and the power of His Resurrection. We hope to be raised to eternal life.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency made the meaning clearer in his talk "The Infinite Power of Hope," from the October 2008 general conference. He said:

Hope is not knowledge, but rather the abiding trust that the Lord will fulfill His promise to us. It is confidence that if we live according to God's laws and the words of His prophets now, we will receive desired blessings in the future. It is believing and expecting that our prayers will be answered. It is manifest in confidence, optimism, enthusiasm, and patient perseverance.

Notice the words. Abiding trust. Confidence. Patient perseverance. This kind of hope is active. It shows up in how we live today. A sailor who trusts the lighthouse does not sit and wait. He steers toward the light.
Where does hope hold us? Think of the lighthouse again. It does not move. Ships can drift, but the light stays on the rock. In the same way, hope is attached to something firm.
Paul called it an anchor.
Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and steadfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;
Sure and steadfast. Those are strong words. Hope is not a thin thread. It is an anchor that holds when the storm is loud.
Moroni gave the same picture. He wrote about what faith leads to.

Wherefore, whoso believeth in God might with surety hope for a better world, yea, even a place at the right hand of God, which hope cometh of faith, maketh an anchor to the souls of men, which would make them sure and steadfast, always abounding in good works, being led to glorify God.

Here is a pattern. Faith leads to hope. Hope becomes an anchor. And an anchored soul is sure and steadfast, always abounding in good works. People who have real hope do not just feel better. They do better. They serve. They keep going.
President Uchtdorf spoke of this in the same talk, "The Infinite Power of Hope." He said:

Hope is a gift of the Spirit. \[See Moroni 8:26.\] It is a hope that through the Atonement of Jesus Christ and the power of His Resurrection, we shall be raised unto life eternal and this because of our faith in the Savior. \[See Moroni 7:41.\] This kind of hope is both a principle of promise as well as a commandment \[see Colossians 1:21–23\], and, as with all commandments, we have the responsibility to make it an active part of our lives and overcome the temptation to lose hope. Hope in our Heavenly Father's merciful plan of happiness leads to peace \[see Romans 15:13\], mercy \[see Psalm 33:22\], rejoicing \[see Romans 12:12\], and gladness. \[See Proverbs 10:28.\] The hope of salvation is like a protective helmet \[see 1 Thessalonians 5:8\]; it is the foundation of our faith \[see Hebrews 11:1; Moroni 7:40\] and an anchor to our souls. \[See Hebrews 6:19; Ether 12:4.\]

Two things stand out. Hope is a gift of the Spirit. We can ask for it. And hope is also a commandment. We are responsible to keep it alive and to resist the pull to lose it. When we feel hope slipping, we can ask for the Spirit and do the small things that feed it. Pray. Read. Serve. Remember what the Lord has done.
Now let us talk about the dark nights. How does hope help when life is hard?
Paul wrote to the Romans about this. He did not say hard things are good. He said they can lead somewhere.

And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.

Tribulation, patience, experience, hope. A chain. Hard times, handled with faith, teach us patience. Patience builds experience with God. And experience with God builds hope. Hope that does not make us ashamed. It is a hope that has been tested.
The prophet Jeremiah gave us an example. He lived through the fall of Jerusalem. He wrote a book of sorrow called Lamentations. In the middle of it, he turned.
This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the Lord's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.

This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. Jeremiah did not feel hope first. He recalled something. He chose to remember the Lord's mercies. And that gave him hope. New every morning. We do not have to carry yesterday's fear into today.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke to those who feel weighed down. In his talk "Broken Things to Mend," from the April 2006 general conference, he said:

This reliance upon the merciful nature of God is at the very center of the gospel Christ taught. I testify that the Savior's Atonement lifts from us not only the burden of our sins but also the burden of our disappointments and sorrows, our heartaches and our despair. \[See Alma 7:11–12.\] From the beginning, trust in such help was to give us both a reason and a way to improve, an incentive to lay down our burdens and take up our salvation.

Heartaches and despair. Elder Holland names them directly. The Atonement is not only for sin. It is for sorrow too. When the waves are high and we feel we are sinking, the light is still there. And we have a Savior who has already felt what we feel.
Some of the darkest nights are the ones we make ourselves. We sin. We drift. We wonder if the light is still on for us.
Alma the Younger knew that night. He had fought against the Church and he was racked with guilt. And then he remembered something his father had taught.

And it came to pass that as I was thus racked with torment, while I was harrowed up by the memory of my many sins, behold, I remembered also to have heard my father prophesy unto the people concerning the coming of one Jesus Christ, a Son of God, to atone for the sins of the world.
Now, as my mind caught hold upon this thought, I cried within my heart: O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me, who am in the gall of bitterness, and am encircled about by the everlasting chains of death.
And now, behold, when I thought this, I could remember my pains no more; yea, I was harrowed up by the memory of my sins no more.

My mind caught hold upon this thought. That is hope at work. Alma was in the dark, and he grabbed the one thing that was true. Jesus Christ can atone. Jesus Christ can have mercy. And when he cried out, the pain left.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland made this promise to anyone who feels beyond reach. In his talk "Prophets in the Land Again," from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

To all of you who think you are lost or without hope, or who think you have done too much that was too wrong for too long, to every one of you who worry that you are stranded somewhere on the wintry plains of life and have wrecked your handcart in the process, this conference calls out Jehovah's unrelenting refrain, '\[My\] hand is stretched out still' \[see Isaiah 5:25; 9:17, 21\]. 'I shall lengthen out mine arm unto them,' He said, '\[and even if they\] deny me; nevertheless, I will be merciful unto them, . . . if they will repent and come unto me; for mine arm is lengthened out all the day long, saith the Lord God of Hosts' \[2 Nephi 28:32\]. His mercy endureth forever, and His hand is stretched out still. His is the pure love of Christ, the charity that never faileth, that compassion which endures even when all other strength disappears \[see Moroni 7:46–47\].
His hand is stretched out still. The light is on. The Lord has not given up on anyone who is willing to come back.
President Uchtdorf said it just as clearly. In his talk "Point of Safe Return," from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

Christ came to save us. If we have taken a wrong course, the Atonement of Jesus Christ can give us the assurance that sin is not a point of no return. A safe return is possible if we will follow God's plan for our salvation. . . . There is always a point of safe return; there is always hope.
There is always hope. Not sometimes. Always. If you have drifted, the harbor is still there. Turn the boat toward the light.
What does hope do for us in daily life? It fills us.
Paul closed a letter to the Romans with a blessing.
Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost.

The God of hope. That is one of His names in this verse. Joy and peace come when we believe. And we can abound in hope, which means overflow with it. And all of this comes through the Holy Ghost. Hope is a gift. We do not make it from nothing. We receive it, and we make room for it.
The Lord also spoke to His people through Jeremiah when they were in a hard season, far from home.
For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the Lord, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.

Thoughts of peace, and not of evil. The Lord is not looking for ways to hurt us. He is planning for our good. An expected end. That means a good outcome that is already on the way. When we cannot see it, we can still trust that He does.
A lighthouse keeper does not wonder if the ships will find the shore. He keeps the lamp burning, because that is his task. The Lord keeps His promises, and our task is to steer toward them.
What does hope look forward to? The greatest promise of all.
Job lost nearly everything. He sat in ashes. His friends blamed him. And in the middle of this, he spoke these words.

For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth: And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God: Whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another; though my reins be consumed within me.

I know that my redeemer liveth. In the darkest place of his life, Job named his hope. It was not a hope that things would be easy. It was a hope that he would see God. Because of Christ, death is not the end.
Nephi told us how to hold this hope.

Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.
A perfect brightness of hope. That is a light we carry. And it leads to eternal life.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when hope carried them through a hard season. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Hannah and the answer to her prayer

blocks.text: Hannah wanted a child more than anything. Year after year she waited. She wept and she prayed at the house of the Lord, and she did not give up. The Lord heard her.

And they rose up in the morning early, and worshipped before the Lord, and returned, and came to their house to Ramah: and Elkanah knew Hannah his wife; and the Lord remembered her. Wherefore it came to pass, when the time was come about after Hannah had conceived, that she bare a son, and called his name Samuel, saying, Because I have asked him of the Lord.

The Lord remembered her. That line is worth pausing on. Hannah had no way to know when her answer would come. But she kept praying, and she kept worshipping. Hope kept her going. And when the answer came, she named her son for it. Samuel, because I have asked.

application.text: Here are a few ways to put this into practice this week.
First, name your lighthouse. Write down one promise of the Lord that you hold on to. It might be Romans 15:13 or Lamentations 3:22–23. Put it where you will see it every morning.
Second, recall the Lord's mercies. Like Jeremiah, take five minutes to write down three times the Lord helped you. When hope feels thin, read the list.
Third, be a light for someone else. Think of one person who feels lost. Reach out. Tell them there is always a point of safe return.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ is the source of all true hope. I know that His Atonement lifts our sins and our sorrows. I have felt His light in my darkest hours, and I know it is real. I know that there is always hope, because He lives. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: Have you ever stayed awake through a long, hard night? The kind where the clock barely moves. Everything feels heavier in the dark. Worries seem bigger. The house is quiet, and your mind is not.
And then, slowly, the window turns gray. A bird starts to sing. The sky grows pale, then gold. You have not fixed a single problem, but somehow you can breathe again.
Why? Because morning is coming. You know it. You can feel it. That is what hope does for the soul.

mainMessage.text: Hope is the sunrise we believe in before we see it. It is not wishful thinking. It is a calm certainty that the Lord's promises will be kept, and that darkness does not last forever.
The gospel teaches that this hope has a source. It is Jesus Christ. Because He rose from the tomb, every night has a morning.

Over the next few minutes, we will look at six things. What hope really is. What it holds onto. What it does in hard times. What it does after we make mistakes. What it gives us each day. And what it points to at the end of life.

blocks.text: First, what is hope? Paul put it beside faith.
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
Things hoped for. Things not seen. We have not seen the sunrise yet, but our faith gives it substance. We know it is on its way.
Moroni recorded his father's words on this. Mormon asked a question that makes us stop and think.

And again, my beloved brethren, I would speak unto you concerning hope. How is it that ye can attain unto faith, save ye shall have hope?
And what is it that ye shall hope for? Behold I say unto you that ye shall have hope through the atonement of Christ and the power of his resurrection, to be raised unto life eternal, and this because of your faith in him according to the promise.

No hope, no faith. That is how closely they are tied. And the object of our hope is clear. The Atonement. The Resurrection. Eternal life. Not a vague good feeling, but a specific promise from a specific Savior.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency described the difference between hope and knowledge in his talk "The Infinite Power of Hope," from the October 2008 general conference. He said:

Hope is not knowledge, but rather the abiding trust that the Lord will fulfill His promise to us. It is confidence that if we live according to God's laws and the words of His prophets now, we will receive desired blessings in the future. It is believing and expecting that our prayers will be answered. It is manifest in confidence, optimism, enthusiasm, and patient perseverance.

We may not know exactly how the morning will look. But we trust the One who made the sun. Notice that President Uchtdorf ties hope to how we live now. If we live according to God's laws, we can expect His blessings. That makes hope something we can act on.
What does hope hold onto? In a long night, you need something that does not move.
Paul used a picture from the sea.
Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and steadfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;
An anchor of the soul. Sure and steadfast. When the night is dark and the water is rough, an anchor keeps the boat from drifting onto the rocks. Hope is that kind of hold.
Moroni told us where the anchor comes from.

Wherefore, whoso believeth in God might with surety hope for a better world, yea, even a place at the right hand of God, which hope cometh of faith, maketh an anchor to the souls of men, which would make them sure and steadfast, always abounding in good works, being led to glorify God.

Hope comes from faith. It anchors us. And anchored people are always abounding in good works. They do not collapse in the dark. They keep serving. They keep doing what is right, because they know the morning is real.
President Uchtdorf explained more in the same talk, "The Infinite Power of Hope." He said:

Hope is a gift of the Spirit. \[See Moroni 8:26.\] It is a hope that through the Atonement of Jesus Christ and the power of His Resurrection, we shall be raised unto life eternal and this because of our faith in the Savior. \[See Moroni 7:41.\] This kind of hope is both a principle of promise as well as a commandment \[see Colossians 1:21–23\], and, as with all commandments, we have the responsibility to make it an active part of our lives and overcome the temptation to lose hope. Hope in our Heavenly Father's merciful plan of happiness leads to peace \[see Romans 15:13\], mercy \[see Psalm 33:22\], rejoicing \[see Romans 12:12\], and gladness. \[See Proverbs 10:28.\] The hope of salvation is like a protective helmet \[see 1 Thessalonians 5:8\]; it is the foundation of our faith \[see Hebrews 11:1; Moroni 7:40\] and an anchor to our souls. \[See Hebrews 6:19; Ether 12:4.\]

A gift of the Spirit. And a commandment. Both. We receive it, and we also have a duty to protect it. If you feel your hope getting dim, ask for it in prayer. And then do the things that keep the Spirit near. Read your scriptures. Go to church. Help someone in need.
What does hope do when the night is hard? It teaches us.
Paul wrote about this to the saints in Rome.

And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.

It is a staircase. Tribulation leads to patience. Patience leads to experience. Experience leads to hope. We do not climb it quickly. But each step builds on the last. And at the top, there is a hope that does not let us down.
The author of Lamentations knew about long nights. He saw his city destroyed. And yet, in the middle of his grief, he wrote this.
This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the Lord's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.

New every morning. That is a sunrise promise. Whatever yesterday held, today comes with new mercy. And he found hope by recalling something. When your heart is heavy, try that. Recall one time the Lord helped you. Say it out loud.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke to those carrying heavy hearts. In his talk "Broken Things to Mend," from the April 2006 general conference, he said:

This reliance upon the merciful nature of God is at the very center of the gospel Christ taught. I testify that the Savior's Atonement lifts from us not only the burden of our sins but also the burden of our disappointments and sorrows, our heartaches and our despair. \[See Alma 7:11–12.\] From the beginning, trust in such help was to give us both a reason and a way to improve, an incentive to lay down our burdens and take up our salvation.
Heartaches and despair. The Savior carries them. Elder Holland says we can lay down our burdens. We do not have to hold the night alone.
Some nights are long because of our own choices. We make mistakes, and then the shame makes the dark even deeper. Where is hope then?
Alma the Younger was in that place. He had done real harm. He was filled with torment. And then one thought came to him.

And it came to pass that as I was thus racked with torment, while I was harrowed up by the memory of my many sins, behold, I remembered also to have heard my father prophesy unto the people concerning the coming of one Jesus Christ, a Son of God, to atone for the sins of the world.
Now, as my mind caught hold upon this thought, I cried within my heart: O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me, who am in the gall of bitterness, and am encircled about by the everlasting chains of death.
And now, behold, when I thought this, I could remember my pains no more; yea, I was harrowed up by the memory of my sins no more.

He remembered. He caught hold. He cried out. And the night was over. This is what hope does for the sinner. It does not say, you are fine. It says, there is a Savior, and He is merciful. Cry out to Him.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland spoke to everyone who feels they have gone too far. In his talk "Prophets in the Land Again," from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

To all of you who think you are lost or without hope, or who think you have done too much that was too wrong for too long, to every one of you who worry that you are stranded somewhere on the wintry plains of life and have wrecked your handcart in the process, this conference calls out Jehovah's unrelenting refrain, '\[My\] hand is stretched out still' \[see Isaiah 5:25; 9:17, 21\]. 'I shall lengthen out mine arm unto them,' He said, '\[and even if they\] deny me; nevertheless, I will be merciful unto them, . . . if they will repent and come unto me; for mine arm is lengthened out all the day long, saith the Lord God of Hosts' \[2 Nephi 28:32\]. His mercy endureth forever, and His hand is stretched out still. His is the pure love of Christ, the charity that never faileth, that compassion which endures even when all other strength disappears \[see Moroni 7:46–47\].
All the day long. His arm is stretched out all the day long. Not for an hour. Not until we have been good enough. All the day long.
President Uchtdorf offered the same assurance in his talk "Point of Safe Return," from the April 2007 general conference. He said:

Christ came to save us. If we have taken a wrong course, the Atonement of Jesus Christ can give us the assurance that sin is not a point of no return. A safe return is possible if we will follow God's plan for our salvation. . . . There is always a point of safe return; there is always hope.
A safe return. If the sun is rising, you can walk toward it. You do not have to wait until you feel ready. You only have to turn around.
What does hope give us each day? Joy, peace, and strength.
Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost.

Abound in hope. That is the picture of an overflowing cup. And it comes by the power of the Holy Ghost. As we believe, joy and peace come. They are not earned by our effort alone. They are gifts that come with faith.
The Lord spoke to the exiles of Judah through Jeremiah. They were far from home, and they felt forgotten. He sent them this message.
For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the Lord, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.

Thoughts of peace. That is how the Lord thinks about you. When you are tempted to believe He is angry or distant, remember this verse. He has a good ending in mind. We may not see it yet. But the sun does not need our permission to rise.
And where does hope finally lead? To the resurrection.
Job sat in ruins. He had lost his children and his health. But hear what he said.

For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth: And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God: Whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another; though my reins be consumed within me.
He looked past his own death and said he would see God. In the longest night of his life, he held on to the morning.
Nephi told us how to keep that hope bright.

Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.
A perfect brightness of hope. That is the light of the morning, carried in us before it arrives. And the promise attached is eternal life.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when hope came after a long night. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Mary at the empty tomb

blocks.text: On the first Easter morning, it was still dark when Mary Magdalene went to the tomb. She had watched Jesus die. She stood outside, weeping. She did not know that the morning she had waited for had already come.

Jesus saith unto her, Woman, why weepest thou? whom seekest thou? She, supposing him to be the gardener, saith unto him, Sir, if thou have borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away. Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master.

She was looking in the wrong direction. Then He said one word. Mary. And everything changed. The sorrow of that night became the joy of that morning. Sometimes we are weeping in the dark and the Lord is already standing beside us. He knows our name.

application.text: Here are some simple steps for this week.
First, greet the morning with a promise. Each day, read one verse that gives you hope. Hebrews 6:19 or Lamentations 3:22–23 are good places to start.
Second, write a recall list. Like the writer of Lamentations, write down three things the Lord has done for you. Keep it where you can read it when the night feels long.
Third, be someone's sunrise. Think of a person who is in a dark place. Send a note, make a call, or sit with them. A little light goes a long way.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ rose from the tomb, and that because of Him every night has a morning. I know that He knows each of us by name. I have felt His hope come into my heart when I needed it most. I know that if we hold on to Him, we will see the sunrise. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

versions.analogy: A sunrise after a long night

opening.text: In the fall, a farmer plants seeds in the ground. Then winter comes. Snow covers the field. Nothing grows. To anyone walking by, the field looks dead.
But the farmer is not worried. He knows what is under the snow. He planted the seeds himself. He knows they are alive, and that spring will come.
That is a good picture of hope. It is trusting what we cannot see, because we know who planted it.

That trust is built on Jesus Christ. He suffered, died, and rose again. Because of Him, the promises are not guesses. They are as sure as the spring.

Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
A seed under the snow is the substance of things hoped for. It is real, though unseen. That is how faith and hope work together. Hope reaches for what is promised, and faith gives it weight.
Mormon explained it to his people with a pointed question.

And again, my beloved brethren, I would speak unto you concerning hope. How is it that ye can attain unto faith, save ye shall have hope?
And what is it that ye shall hope for? Behold I say unto you that ye shall have hope through the atonement of Christ and the power of his resurrection, to be raised unto life eternal, and this because of your faith in him according to the promise.
Without hope, there is no faith. And the thing we hope for is named. Through the Atonement of Christ and the power of His Resurrection, we hope to be raised to eternal life. That is the harvest.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency taught what hope is and is not. In his talk "The Infinite Power of Hope," from the October 2008 general conference, he said:

Hope is not knowledge, but rather the abiding trust that the Lord will fulfill His promise to us. It is believing and expecting that our prayers will be answered. It is manifest in confidence, optimism, enthusiasm, and patient perseverance.
Patient perseverance. A farmer does not dig up the seeds in January. He waits. And while he waits, he keeps the fences mended and the tools ready. Hope is not idle. It prepares for the harvest.
What is hope rooted in? The seed needs soil. Hope needs something firm.
Paul wrote that our hope is like an anchor.
Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and steadfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;
Sure and steadfast. It reaches within the veil, which means it reaches into the presence of God. It is not tied to what happens in this world. It is tied to heaven.
Moroni wrote of the same anchor, and he linked it to faith.

Wherefore, whoso believeth in God might with surety hope for a better world, yea, even a place at the right hand of God, which hope cometh of faith, maketh an anchor to the souls of men, which would make them sure and steadfast, always abounding in good works, being led to glorify God.
Hope cometh of faith. Seeds do not grow from nothing. Hope grows from faith in God. And the fruit is good works. People with this kind of hope do not just wait for spring. They tend the field.
President Uchtdorf said more in "The Infinite Power of Hope." He said:

Hope is a gift of the Spirit. \[See Moroni 8:26.\] It is a hope that through the Atonement of Jesus Christ and the power of His Resurrection, we shall be raised unto life eternal and this because of our faith in the Savior. \[See Moroni 7:41.\] This kind of hope is both a principle of promise as well as a commandment \[see Colossians 1:21–23\], and, as with all commandments, we have the responsibility to make it an active part of our lives and overcome the temptation to lose hope. Hope in our Heavenly Father's merciful plan of happiness leads to peace \[see Romans 15:13\], mercy \[see Psalm 33:22\], rejoicing \[see Romans 12:12\], and gladness. \[See Proverbs 10:28.\] The hope of salvation is like a protective helmet \[see 1 Thessalonians 5:8\]; it is the foundation of our faith \[see Hebrews 11:1; Moroni 7:40\] and an anchor to our souls. \[See Hebrews 6:19; Ether 12:4.\]

The foundation of our faith. An anchor. A helmet. A gift. A commandment. President Uchtdorf gives hope many pictures because it does many jobs. And the word commandment is worth noting. We are asked to keep hope. That means we have to protect it, as a farmer protects a field.
How does hope grow in the hard seasons? Often, it grows there best.
Paul described it as a process.

And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.

Tribulation, patience, experience, hope. The winter does its work. Under the cold, roots form. After a hard season, we have more hope than we had before, because we have seen the Lord bring us through. Experience builds hope.
The writer of Lamentations lived through a bitter winter. His city was in ruins. And he wrote this.
This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the Lord's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.

This I recall to my mind. He did not feel hopeful. He chose to remember. He called to mind the Lord's mercies. And that choice gave him hope. When your field looks bare, remember who planted the seed. Remember what the Lord has already done.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke of the same mercy. In his talk "Broken Things to Mend," from the April 2006 general conference, he said:

This reliance upon the merciful nature of God is at the very center of the gospel Christ taught. I testify that the Savior's Atonement lifts from us not only the burden of our sins but also the burden of our disappointments and sorrows, our heartaches and our despair. \[See Alma 7:11–12.\] From the beginning, trust in such help was to give us both a reason and a way to improve, an incentive to lay down our burdens and take up our salvation.
A reason and a way. Hope gives us a reason to keep going, and a way to do it. And we can lay down our burdens. We do not have to carry the whole winter on our back.
What if the field was damaged by our own hands? What if we stepped on the seedlings, or forgot to water them for a season?
Alma the Younger knew that feeling. He had led many away from the faith. He was in agony over what he had done. But he remembered something that gave him hope.

And it came to pass that as I was thus racked with torment, while I was harrowed up by the memory of my many sins, behold, I remembered also to have heard my father prophesy unto the people concerning the coming of one Jesus Christ, a Son of God, to atone for the sins of the world.
Now, as my mind caught hold upon this thought, I cried within my heart: O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me, who am in the gall of bitterness, and am encircled about by the everlasting chains of death.
And now, behold, when I thought this, I could remember my pains no more; yea, I was harrowed up by the memory of my sins no more.

One thought. One cry. And the torment lifted. Alma did not have a long speech. He caught hold of the truth that Christ would atone, and he asked for mercy. That is the seed of hope for every person who has fallen.
Elder Holland described the reach of that mercy. In his talk "Prophets in the Land Again," from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

To all of you who think you are lost or without hope, or who think you have done too much that was too wrong for too long, to every one of you who worry that you are stranded somewhere on the wintry plains of life and have wrecked your handcart in the process, this conference calls out Jehovah's unrelenting refrain, '\[My\] hand is stretched out still' \[see Isaiah 5:25; 9:17, 21\]. 'I shall lengthen out mine arm unto them,' He said, '\[and even if they\] deny me; nevertheless, I will be merciful unto them, . . . if they will repent and come unto me; for mine arm is lengthened out all the day long, saith the Lord God of Hosts' \[2 Nephi 28:32\]. His mercy endureth forever, and His hand is stretched out still. His is the pure love of Christ, the charity that never faileth, that compassion which endures even when all other strength disappears \[see Moroni 7:46–47\].

The wintry plains of life. Elder Holland even uses winter as his picture. And he says the hand of the Lord is stretched out still. A damaged field can be replanted. A wrecked handcart can be mended. The Lord does not walk away.
President Uchtdorf gave the same message in his talk "Point of Safe Return," from the April 2007 general conference. He said:

Christ came to save us. If we have taken a wrong course, the Atonement of Jesus Christ can give us the assurance that sin is not a point of no return. A safe return is possible if we will follow God's plan for our salvation. . . . There is always a point of safe return; there is always hope.
Always. If you are listening and you feel you have gone too far, hear it again. There is always a point of safe return.
How does hope fill our days? It brings fruit now, not only later.
Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost.

Joy and peace are early fruit. A person with real hope often has a lightness that others notice. Not because their life is easy, but because they trust the harvest. And notice how it comes. Through the power of the Holy Ghost. We ask, and He fills.
The Lord told His people in Babylon, who were far from home and in a long winter of their own, what He was thinking about them.
For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the Lord, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.
He knows the thoughts that He thinks toward us. They are thoughts of peace. The expected end is the harvest. It is coming. And in the meantime, we can live with peace in the cold.
What is the harvest? Resurrection, and life with God.
Job said it from the middle of the worst winter a man could imagine.

For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth: And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God: Whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another; though my reins be consumed within me.
I know that my redeemer liveth. That is the seed of everything. Because He lives, we will live. Even after the body is gone, Job says, in my flesh shall I see God. That is the harvest.
And Nephi tells us how to keep going until we get there.

Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.

Press forward. Hold a perfect brightness of hope. Feast on the word of Christ. That is how a farmer lives through winter. He keeps working. He keeps believing. And in the end, he eats from what he planted.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they kept hoping against the odds. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Abraham hoped against hope

blocks.text: Abraham and Sarah were old. They had no children. By every natural measure, the promise of a great family had passed. And yet Paul says of Abraham:

Who against hope believed in hope, that he might become the father of many nations, according to that which was spoken, So shall thy seed be. And being not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sara's womb: He staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God; And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform.

Against hope, he believed in hope. That means that when every sign pointed the other way, he held on to the promise. He gave glory to God while he waited. He was fully persuaded that God could do what He said. The seed was under the snow, and Abraham trusted the Planter.

application.text: Here are some steps to take this week.
First, tend the field. Pick one daily action that feeds your hope. Scripture study, a short prayer, or a walk to think about the Lord's goodness. Keep it up even when you feel no change.
Second, remember who planted the seed. Write down one promise of the Lord to you. Then write one way He has kept a promise in the past. Put both where you will see them.
Third, share some seed. Is there someone who feels their field is bare? Take a few minutes this week to tell them what gives you hope.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ is the seed of all our hope. I know that He lives, and that He keeps His promises. I have seen Him bring life out of hard seasons. I know that if we trust Him and keep going, we will see the harvest. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: Think of a time you came home late at night. Maybe you were a teenager and had missed curfew. Maybe you were an adult, tired after a long trip. You turned onto your street, and from far away you saw it. A light on the porch.
Someone had left it on for you. And just seeing it changed how you felt. You were not lost. You were expected. Someone was waiting.
That is a picture of hope. A light left on for us, by someone who loves us and wants us home.

mainMessage.text: The gospel teaches that hope is more than a good feeling. It is a trust that our Heavenly Father keeps the light on. It is confidence that His promises are real, and that Jesus Christ has made a way for us to come home.
When life is confusing or painful, hope tells us the light is still on. When we have gone astray, hope tells us the door is not locked.
We will look at six things. What hope is. What it holds to. How it helps in trouble. How it welcomes us home after mistakes. What it gives us along the way. And the home it points to.

blocks.text: Let us start with a clear description. What is hope?
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
Things hoped for. Things not seen. We cannot always see our heavenly home from where we are. But faith lets us know the light is on.
Mormon taught his people about this. His words were recorded by his son Moroni.

And again, my beloved brethren, I would speak unto you concerning hope. How is it that ye can attain unto faith, save ye shall have hope?
And what is it that ye shall hope for? Behold I say unto you that ye shall have hope through the atonement of Christ and the power of his resurrection, to be raised unto life eternal, and this because of your faith in him according to the promise.
Hope and faith go together. And what is the home we hope for? Eternal life, made possible by the Atonement and the Resurrection. That is the light on the porch.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency described hope this way in his talk "The Infinite Power of Hope," from the October 2008 general conference:

Hope is not knowledge, but rather the abiding trust that the Lord will fulfill His promise to us. It is confidence that if we live according to God's laws and the words of His prophets now, we will receive desired blessings in the future. It is believing and expecting that our prayers will be answered. It is manifest in confidence, optimism, enthusiasm, and patient perseverance.

Believing and expecting that our prayers will be answered. That is how a traveler feels when the porch light is in view. Not certainty about every detail. But trust that home is there, and that we are welcome.
What does hope hold on to? It holds to something that does not change.
Paul called hope an anchor.
Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and steadfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;

Within the veil. Our hope reaches all the way to the presence of God. It is not fastened to the things of this world, which come and go. It is fastened to heaven. So when the storms of life shake us, the anchor holds.
Moroni explained the same truth.

Wherefore, whoso believeth in God might with surety hope for a better world, yea, even a place at the right hand of God, which hope cometh of faith, maketh an anchor to the souls of men, which would make them sure and steadfast, always abounding in good works, being led to glorify God.

With surety. That means with certainty. A better world. A place at the right hand of God. That is home. And those who hope for it are led to glorify God and do good along the way. A traveler who knows the porch light is on walks with purpose.
President Uchtdorf said more in the same talk. In "The Infinite Power of Hope," he said:

Hope is a gift of the Spirit. \[See Moroni 8:26.\] It is a hope that through the Atonement of Jesus Christ and the power of His Resurrection, we shall be raised unto life eternal and this because of our faith in the Savior. \[See Moroni 7:41.\] This kind of hope is both a principle of promise as well as a commandment \[see Colossians 1:21–23\], and, as with all commandments, we have the responsibility to make it an active part of our lives and overcome the temptation to lose hope. Hope in our Heavenly Father's merciful plan of happiness leads to peace \[see Romans 15:13\], mercy \[see Psalm 33:22\], rejoicing \[see Romans 12:12\], and gladness. \[See Proverbs 10:28.\] The hope of salvation is like a protective helmet \[see 1 Thessalonians 5:8\]; it is the foundation of our faith \[see Hebrews 11:1; Moroni 7:40\] and an anchor to our souls. \[See Hebrews 6:19; Ether 12:4.\]

Hope leads to peace, mercy, rejoicing, and gladness. Those are the things we feel when we see the light and know we are almost home. And notice that hope is a commandment. We are asked to keep it burning, and to resist the voice that says it is hopeless.
What about the hard stretches of the road? Does hope help there?
Paul said yes, and he explained how.

And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.

Tribulation builds patience. Patience builds experience. Experience builds hope. Each hard mile teaches us something about the Lord's faithfulness. And by the end, we have a hope that is not ashamed, because we have seen the Lord come through.
The writer of Lamentations traveled a long and sorrowful road. He wrote of grief and ruin. But in the middle of it, he found a light.
This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the Lord's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
Great is thy faithfulness. The light on the porch is steady. It does not flicker with our moods. Even when we feel unworthy or far away, the Lord's compassions fail not.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this about the Savior's care. In his talk "Broken Things to Mend," from the April 2006 general conference, he said:

This reliance upon the merciful nature of God is at the very center of the gospel Christ taught. I testify that the Savior's Atonement lifts from us not only the burden of our sins but also the burden of our disappointments and sorrows, our heartaches and our despair. \[See Alma 7:11–12.\] From the beginning, trust in such help was to give us both a reason and a way to improve, an incentive to lay down our burdens and take up our salvation.

An incentive to lay down our burdens. When we get home, we set down our bags. The Savior invites us to do that now. We do not have to carry our heartaches and despair all the way. We can give them to Him.
Now the hardest question. What if we are the reason we are lost? What if we left on our own, and now we are not sure we can go back?
The prodigal feeling is common. We think the door is closed. But Alma the Younger discovered it was not.

And it came to pass that as I was thus racked with torment, while I was harrowed up by the memory of my many sins, behold, I remembered also to have heard my father prophesy unto the people concerning the coming of one Jesus Christ, a Son of God, to atone for the sins of the world.
Now, as my mind caught hold upon this thought, I cried within my heart: O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me, who am in the gall of bitterness, and am encircled about by the everlasting chains of death.
And now, behold, when I thought this, I could remember my pains no more; yea, I was harrowed up by the memory of my sins no more.
He remembered what his father had taught. He caught hold of it. And he cried out inside his heart for mercy. The light was on the whole time. Alma only had to turn toward it.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland spoke to every person who thinks the door is locked. In his talk "Prophets in the Land Again," from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

To all of you who think you are lost or without hope, or who think you have done too much that was too wrong for too long, to every one of you who worry that you are stranded somewhere on the wintry plains of life and have wrecked your handcart in the process, this conference calls out Jehovah's unrelenting refrain, '\[My\] hand is stretched out still' \[see Isaiah 5:25; 9:17, 21\]. 'I shall lengthen out mine arm unto them,' He said, '\[and even if they\] deny me; nevertheless, I will be merciful unto them, . . . if they will repent and come unto me; for mine arm is lengthened out all the day long, saith the Lord God of Hosts' \[2 Nephi 28:32\]. His mercy endureth forever, and His hand is stretched out still. His is the pure love of Christ, the charity that never faileth, that compassion which endures even when all other strength disappears \[see Moroni 7:46–47\].
His arm is lengthened out all the day long. Think of a parent standing on the porch, arm stretched toward the road. That is how the Lord waits for us.
President Uchtdorf said it plainly. In his talk "Point of Safe Return," from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

Christ came to save us. If we have taken a wrong course, the Atonement of Jesus Christ can give us the assurance that sin is not a point of no return. A safe return is possible if we will follow God's plan for our salvation. . . . There is always a point of safe return; there is always hope.
A safe return. Always possible. The first step is to turn toward the light.
What does hope give us on the way? Joy and peace that we can feel before we arrive.
Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost.
All joy and peace in believing. Not after we arrive. In believing. Right now, as we walk. And it comes through the Holy Ghost. If you want more hope, ask for the Spirit. He is the one who fills us.
The Lord sent a letter through Jeremiah to people who were far from home and far from comfort.
For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the Lord, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.

Thoughts of peace. That is what He thinks about us, even when we are far off. An expected end means He has a good ending planned, and He expects it to happen. The porch light was lit before we left. It will still be lit when we return.
What is the home we are walking toward? It is life with God, and the resurrection.
Job saw it from a place of deep pain. He lost almost everything, but he never lost sight of his home.

For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth: And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God: Whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another; though my reins be consumed within me.
I know that my redeemer liveth. Job names who is waiting at the end of the road. He will stand upon the earth. And Job will see Him with his own eyes. That is the light we are walking toward.
Nephi gave us the way to keep walking.

Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.
Press forward. Keep a perfect brightness of hope. Feast on the word of Christ. And the Father says, you shall have eternal life. That is the welcome waiting at the door.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when hope held them up in grief. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Martha and the resurrection

blocks.text: Martha's brother Lazarus had died. Jesus came, but He came after the funeral. Martha went out to meet Him, and she said what many of us have felt.

Then said Martha unto Jesus, Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died. But I know, that even now, whatsoever thou wilt ask of God, God will give it thee. Jesus saith unto her, Thy brother shall rise again. Martha saith unto him, I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day. Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this? She saith unto him, Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world.

Martha was honest about her pain. If thou hadst been here. But she also said, I know. She knew that her brother would rise again. She had a light on in her heart even on the worst day of her life. And Jesus met her there. He said, I am the resurrection, and the life. That is the porch light, and He is the one who lit it.

application.text: Here are some steps for this week.

First, turn toward the light. If you have been avoiding the Lord because you feel unworthy, take one small step. Pray for five minutes. Tell Him you want to come back. He is waiting with an outstretched arm.
Second, carry a light verse. Choose one verse from this talk, such as Lamentations 3:22–23 or Jeremiah 29:11. Write it on a card and keep it with you.
Third, leave a light on for someone. Think of a friend or family member who has drifted. Send a kind message this week. Let them know they are welcome.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that my Heavenly Father keeps a light on for each of us. I know that Jesus Christ is the resurrection and the life. I have felt His welcome when I needed it most. I know that there is always a point of safe return. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: Imagine you are hiking a long mountain trail. The path climbs through trees. Your legs ache. Your pack feels heavier with each step. You cannot see the top. Around a bend, you pass a small wooden sign. It says, Summit, two miles.
You are still tired. The hill is still steep. But something has changed. You now know the top is real, and you know how far it is. And that is enough to put one foot in front of the other.
That sign is what hope is. It does not carry us up the mountain. It tells us the climb is worth it.

mainMessage.text: Hope is a quiet strength in the gospel. It is the trust that God will do what He promised. It makes us keep climbing when we are weary, and it makes us pick ourselves up when we fall.
That hope is built on Jesus Christ. He has already been to the top. He climbed the hardest road of all, and He holds out His hand to us.
We will look at six parts. What hope is. What it hangs on to. How it carries us in hard times. How it helps us after we stumble. What it brings along the trail. And what waits at the summit.

blocks.text: First, what is hope? Paul put it beside faith.
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
The summit is a thing hoped for. We cannot see it from the trailhead. But faith treats it as real. Faith gives hope its footing.
Mormon taught about this in a letter to his son, and Moroni wrote it down.

And again, my beloved brethren, I would speak unto you concerning hope. How is it that ye can attain unto faith, save ye shall have hope?
And what is it that ye shall hope for? Behold I say unto you that ye shall have hope through the atonement of Christ and the power of his resurrection, to be raised unto life eternal, and this because of your faith in him according to the promise.
What do we hope for? Life eternal, through the Atonement and the Resurrection. That is the summit. And no faith can reach it without hope along the way.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency gave a plain definition in his talk "The Infinite Power of Hope," from the October 2008 general conference. He said:

Hope is not knowledge, but rather the abiding trust that the Lord will fulfill His promise to us. It is confidence that if we live according to God's laws and the words of His prophets now, we will receive desired blessings in the future. It is believing and expecting that our prayers will be answered. It is manifest in confidence, optimism, enthusiasm, and patient perseverance.

We do not climb because we have already been to the top. We climb because we trust the One who has. That is the difference between knowledge and hope. And the habits that make hope strong are plain. Live by God's laws. Follow the prophets. Pray, and expect an answer. Keep going with patience.
What does hope hold on to when the trail gets steep? It holds on to an anchor point, like a rope fixed to the rock.
Paul wrote about it this way.
Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and steadfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;
Sure and steadfast. A climber clips into a fixed line so that a slip does not become a fall. Hope is a line like that. It reaches within the veil, to the very presence of God.
Moroni described the same anchor.

Wherefore, whoso believeth in God might with surety hope for a better world, yea, even a place at the right hand of God, which hope cometh of faith, maketh an anchor to the souls of men, which would make them sure and steadfast, always abounding in good works, being led to glorify God.

Hope cometh of faith. It is not something we conjure up. It grows when we believe in God. And it makes us sure and steadfast. Not careless, but steady. People who are anchored do not freeze on a ledge. They keep climbing, and they help others along. They abound in good works.
President Uchtdorf spoke of this in the same talk. In "The Infinite Power of Hope," he said:

Hope is a gift of the Spirit. \[See Moroni 8:26.\] It is a hope that through the Atonement of Jesus Christ and the power of His Resurrection, we shall be raised unto life eternal and this because of our faith in the Savior. \[See Moroni 7:41.\] This kind of hope is both a principle of promise as well as a commandment \[see Colossians 1:21–23\], and, as with all commandments, we have the responsibility to make it an active part of our lives and overcome the temptation to lose hope. Hope in our Heavenly Father's merciful plan of happiness leads to peace \[see Romans 15:13\], mercy \[see Psalm 33:22\], rejoicing \[see Romans 12:12\], and gladness. \[See Proverbs 10:28.\] The hope of salvation is like a protective helmet \[see 1 Thessalonians 5:8\]; it is the foundation of our faith \[see Hebrews 11:1; Moroni 7:40\] and an anchor to our souls. \[See Hebrews 6:19; Ether 12:4.\]

A helmet and an anchor. Both are gear for climbers. President Uchtdorf says hope protects us and holds us. And he reminds us that we have a responsibility to keep it. When the temptation comes to quit, we do not have to give in. We can ask for the Spirit, and we can keep climbing.
How does hope carry us in hard times? It turns the climb into growth.

And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.

Paul describes a trail with four stages. Tribulation. Patience. Experience. Hope. Each hard stretch makes us stronger for the next. A hiker who has climbed a steep hill once is less afraid of the next one. We are the same. Each time the Lord helps us through, our hope grows.
The writer of Lamentations had come through a time of terrible loss. He wrote of grief and darkness. But he found a footing.
This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the Lord's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.

New every morning. Hikers know that each day on the trail begins with a fresh start. Yesterday's blisters are real, but today has its own mercy. And the writer found hope by remembering. When the trail is steep, recall what the Lord has already carried you through.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke to those who feel worn out. In his talk "Broken Things to Mend," from the April 2006 general conference, he said:

This reliance upon the merciful nature of God is at the very center of the gospel Christ taught. I testify that the Savior's Atonement lifts from us not only the burden of our sins but also the burden of our disappointments and sorrows, our heartaches and our despair. \[See Alma 7:11–12.\] From the beginning, trust in such help was to give us both a reason and a way to improve, an incentive to lay down our burdens and take up our salvation.
Lay down our burdens. A heavy pack can be shared. The Savior has taken up our sorrows already. We can set down the weight that is not ours to carry, and keep climbing with lighter steps.
Every hiker slips at some point. A rock rolls. A foot slides. The question is whether we get up. And what if the slip was our own fault? What if we left the trail on purpose?
Alma the Younger had wandered far off. He had fought against the Church. But when he was at his lowest, hope found him.

And it came to pass that as I was thus racked with torment, while I was harrowed up by the memory of my many sins, behold, I remembered also to have heard my father prophesy unto the people concerning the coming of one Jesus Christ, a Son of God, to atone for the sins of the world.
Now, as my mind caught hold upon this thought, I cried within my heart: O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me, who am in the gall of bitterness, and am encircled about by the everlasting chains of death.
And now, behold, when I thought this, I could remember my pains no more; yea, I was harrowed up by the memory of my sins no more.

He caught hold. Like a climber who grabs a rope as he slides. Alma grabbed the thought of Jesus Christ and cried out for mercy. The torment ended. You can do the same. The rope is there. You only have to reach for it.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland spoke of how far the Lord's reach is. In his talk "Prophets in the Land Again," from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

To all of you who think you are lost or without hope, or who think you have done too much that was too wrong for too long, to every one of you who worry that you are stranded somewhere on the wintry plains of life and have wrecked your handcart in the process, this conference calls out Jehovah's unrelenting refrain, '\[My\] hand is stretched out still' \[see Isaiah 5:25; 9:17, 21\]. 'I shall lengthen out mine arm unto them,' He said, '\[and even if they\] deny me; nevertheless, I will be merciful unto them, . . . if they will repent and come unto me; for mine arm is lengthened out all the day long, saith the Lord God of Hosts' \[2 Nephi 28:32\]. His mercy endureth forever, and His hand is stretched out still. His is the pure love of Christ, the charity that never faileth, that compassion which endures even when all other strength disappears \[see Moroni 7:46–47\].

His hand is stretched out still. A hand reaching down from the next ledge. Elder Holland says it is there for the one who has wrecked their handcart, and for the one who thinks they have done too much for too long. No one is out of reach.
President Uchtdorf said it in a few clear words. In his talk "Point of Safe Return," from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

Christ came to save us. If we have taken a wrong course, the Atonement of Jesus Christ can give us the assurance that sin is not a point of no return. A safe return is possible if we will follow God's plan for our salvation. . . . There is always a point of safe return; there is always hope.
A point of safe return. On any trail, you can turn back to the last marker you know. The Lord has set markers for us. Repentance is the way back.
What does hope bring along the trail? Joy and peace, even before the top.
Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost.

The God of hope. Joy and peace in believing. Not after the summit, but on the way. A good hiker sings. A good hiker notices the view. In the same way, hope lets us enjoy the climb. And it comes through the Holy Ghost. We can pray for it each morning.
The Lord sent this word to the people of Judah when they were in exile.
For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the Lord, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.

He knows the thoughts He thinks toward us. Peace, not evil. An expected end. That is the summit. It is not a trick or a trap. It is the good outcome the Lord has in mind for each of us. When the trail is long and the clouds are low, we can trust that He knows where it leads.
What waits at the top? Resurrection, and the presence of God.
Job was on a different kind of trail. His was the trail of loss and sickness. And from the middle of it, he said this.

For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth: And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God: Whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another; though my reins be consumed within me.
I know that my redeemer liveth. That is the summit that Job could see in the middle of the storm. He would see God, in his own flesh, with his own eyes.
Nephi told us how to keep climbing until we get there.

Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.
Press forward. A perfect brightness of hope. Feast on the word of Christ. And you shall have eternal life. That is the top of the mountain.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when hope gave them strength to keep climbing. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Enos and the voice of forgiveness

blocks.text: Enos went into the forest to hunt. But the words of his father about eternal life had sunk deep into his heart. He could not shake them. So he knelt down and prayed.

And my soul hungered; and I kneeled down before my Maker, and I cried unto him in mighty prayer and supplication for mine own soul; and all the day long did I cry unto him; yea, and when the night came I did still raise my voice high that it reached the heavens. And there came a voice unto me, saying: Enos, thy sins are forgiven thee, and thou shalt be blessed.

Enos hoped for something he could not yet see. He prayed all day and into the night. He did not stop at the first sign of silence. And the answer came. Thy sins are forgiven thee. Hope is not just a feeling. It is a reason to keep praying and keep climbing until the answer comes.

application.text: Here are some steps for this week.
First, set a trail marker. Choose a small goal that you will finish this week. Read a chapter. Make an apology. Attend a meeting. Each finished step builds hope for the next.
Second, grab the rope. If you feel you have slipped, say a short prayer today. Tell the Lord you want to come back. He is already reaching toward you.
Third, walk with someone. Is there a friend who is struggling up the same hill? Offer to walk with them. Climbing is easier with company.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ has climbed the hardest road for us. I know that His hand is stretched out still, and that He will lift us if we reach for Him. I have felt hope return to me when I thought it was gone. I know that there is always hope. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.
